hints: Expand sin4x as 2sin2x cos2x, then use sin2x=2sinx cosx.
Replace cos2x by 2cos²x−1 and factor to obtain the stated right side.
walkthrough:
Expand $\sin(2x)$ using $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x\cos x$:
$$\sin(4x) = 2(2\sin x\cos x)\cos(2x) = 4\sin x\cos x\cos(2x)$$

Substitute the double-angle formula $\cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x - 1$:
$$\sin(4x) = 4\sin x\cos x\left(2\cos^2 x - 1\right)$$

Distribute $\cos x$ into the bracket:
$$\cos x\left(2\cos^2 x - 1\right) = 2\cos^3 x - \cos x$$
$$\sin(4x) = 4\sin x\left(2\cos^3 x - \cos x\right)$$

ai_rubric.Trigonometric Identities: Applies a double-angle formula to expand $\sin4x$, e.g. $2\sin2x\cos2x$; Applies a double-angle formula to derive an expression in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, e.g. $4\sin x\cos x(2\cos^2x-1)$; Concludes with $\sin4x=4\sin x(2\cos^3x-\cos x)$.

hints: Insert the identity from part (a) and multiply by cos³x to form powers cos⁶x and cos⁴x with sinx.
Use u=cosx, transform the limits 0 and π/4, and evaluate the two power integrals exactly.
walkthrough:
Substitute the identity $\sin(4x) = 4\sin x\left(2\cos^3 x - \cos x\right)$ into the integrand:
$$\cos^3 x\sin(4x) = \cos^3 x\left(8\sin x\cos^3 x - 4\sin x\cos x\right) = 8\sin x\cos^6 x - 4\sin x\cos^4 x$$

Integrate with respect to $x$ using the reverse chain rule or substitution $u = \cos x$ (so $\mathrm{d}u = -\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x$):
$$\int \left(8\sin x\cos^6 x - 4\sin x\cos^4 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{8}{7}\cos^7 x + \dfrac{4}{5}\cos^5 x$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$ where $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:
$$\cos^5\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^5 = \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}$$
$$\cos^7\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^7 = \dfrac{1}{8\sqrt{2}}$$
$$-\dfrac{8}{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{8\sqrt{2}}\right) + \dfrac{4}{5}\left(\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{7\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{-5 + 7}{35\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2}{35\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{35}$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the lower limit $x = 0$ where $\cos(0) = 1$:
$$-\dfrac{8}{7}(1^7) + \dfrac{4}{5}(1^5) = -\dfrac{8}{7} + \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{-40 + 28}{35} = -\dfrac{12}{35}$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{35} - \left(-\dfrac{12}{35}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} + 12}{35}$$

ai_rubric.Integration: Applies the identity to derive $p\int\sin x\cos^6x\,dx+q\int\sin x\cos^4x\,dx$; Derives $-\dfrac87\cos^7x+\dfrac45\cos^5x$; Concludes with $\dfrac{\sqrt2+12}{35}$.
